item.title: Guam Board of Education chair wants oversight hearing on Public Health's requirements for schools
item.description: Guam Board of Education Chairperson Judith Guthertz said Monday she would like the chair of the Legislature’s Committee on Education to call an immediate oversight hearing for the Department of Public Health’s Environmental Health Division. Guthertz said she was upset because people on a radio talk show were making fun of the Education Department for installing air conditioning in school restrooms
item.content:encoded:
Guam Board of Education Chairperson Judith Guthertz said Monday she would like the chair of the Legislature’s Committee on Education to call an immediate oversight hearing for the Department of Public Health’s Environmental Health Division.

Guthertz said she was upset because people on a radio talk show were making fun of the Education Department for installing air conditioning in school restrooms, but the department is merely complying with Public Health regulations.

She said the oversight hearing should be called, “with the goal of determining whether or not these regulations make sense. That is the source of many of the difficulties that we have experienced over the last few months.”

The Tiyan High School campus, which also housed students from Simon Sanchez High School, was closed by Public Health shortly after the school year began in August, leading to double sessions and emergency repairs.

She wanted the public to know the idea for cooler bathrooms did not come from the Education Department.

“People in the community don't understand this, that we have to honor those regulations, no matter whether or not they make sense,” she said, questioning whether air conditioning in restrooms would affect student learning. “I take great exception to the lack of clarification on the part of the media that do not understand where these regulations come from.”

She said air conditioning is also being installed at University of Guam restrooms.

“Can you imagine what the costs are going to be for DOE? We have to do this in every school, in every bathroom, and at the university and at GCC. Why could we not put ceiling fans? Would that not help?” she asked. “Split units, the cost of retrofitting the electrical requirements, the installation costs, the material costs, the equipment costs. I'd rather use that money in the classrooms.”

Because the matter could not be addressed during Monday’s emergency meeting for the department’s spending plan, Guthertz asked that it be placed on the board agenda for the upcoming Nov. 17 meeting.

The board will consider whether to ask the superintendent to request an oversight hearing on the Public Health requirements.

item.title: DPW announces Simon Sanchez High School project to move forward through two separate procurement processes
item.description: The Department of Public Works announced that the Simon Sanchez High School project is moving forward through two separate procurement processes, but neither demolition nor construction has officially begun. Under the first procurement process, Public Works has completed its part of the bidding process for demolishing the existing Simon Sanchez High School Campus, and the Office of the Attorney Ge
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Works announced that the Simon Sanchez High School project is moving forward through two separate procurement processes, but neither demolition nor construction has officially begun.

Under the first procurement process, Public Works has completed its part of the bidding process for demolishing the existing Simon Sanchez High School Campus, and the Office of the Attorney General has reviewed and cleared the demolition bid documents. However, Public Works is still waiting for GDOE to authorize the architect, TRMA, to finish the remaining work and release the documents needed. Once GDOE accepts, Public Works says it is ready to advertise the demolition bidding and move forward.

For the second procurement and the construction of the new school, Public Works has completed preparing the request for proposals for the school’s construction through a public-private partnership. The proposal package still needs final review by the Attorney General's Office before it is issued. Public Works plans to turn over the procurement package to the incoming administration for consideration and implementation.

item.title: Selection committee to interview six MVA director candidates
item.description: The Marianas Visitors Authority board of directors has formed a selection committee to evaluate six applicants for the agency's vacant managing director position. The action came during a special board meeting Monday where directors addressed the recently closed job vacancy announcement for MVA's top executive post.
item.content:encoded:
The Marianas Visitors Authority board of directors has formed a selection committee to evaluate six applicants for the agency's vacant managing director position.

The action came during a special board meeting Monday where directors addressed the recently closed job vacancy announcement for MVA's top executive post.

Acting Managing Director Judy Torres told board members that the application period ended last week.

The board approved the creation of a selection committee tasked with reviewing applications, conducting interviews and recommending a candidate to the full board.

The committee consists of board members Sakuro Gerrard, Chris Nelson and Joe Guerrero, along with Torres and MVA Human Resources Manager Tina Matsunaga.

Acting Board Chair Vicky Benavente said the committee will begin its work as soon as possible.

"The selection committee will meet as soon as possible and conduct interviews and evaluations and will make a recommendation to the whole board," Benavente said.

Speaking with reporters following the meeting, Torres declined to identify the applicants.

Asked whether MVA has established a target date for hiring its next managing director, Torres said the timeline will depend on how quickly the committee can complete its review process.

"It all depends on how soon the committee can review the applications and set up a date to proceed," she said.

No timeline for a final hiring decision was announced.

item.title: France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks
item.description: France is accusing Iran of having launched a series of destructive cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure in October. item.content:encoded:
France is accusing Iran of having launched a series of destructive cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure in October.

According to the French National Cybersecurity Agency, ANSSI, Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites in France, from supermarkets to butcher shops, turning up the temperature in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.

They also targeted several small hydroelectric power plants, resulting in "moderate effects," wrote ANSSI in its press release.

The hacking campaign was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," said French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot. He said it "marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people."

The Paris Prosecutor's Office has opened its own investigation into the Iranian cyber unit, Shahid Kaveh, which the French government is linking to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "The Paris Public Prosecutor's Office is requesting the issuance of international arrest warrants," the office said in a statement.

The attacks on French industrial controllers are part of a larger trend . In 2026 alone, hackers have targeted refrigeration controllers from Europe to Israel and the United States.

Grocery stores in European countries including Sweden and Ireland were hit in similar attacks last week.

In a separate incident in France, employees at a major French blood bank had to act fast to save blood samples from heating up when their refrigeration system was hit last week, prompting international calls for the health sector to protect its lifesaving products from spoiling.

In Israel in the spring, suspected Iranian hackers going by the name of "Cyber Isnaad Front" claimed responsibility for sabotaging an industrial food processing plant, including infecting its corporate computers with malware, taking over office printers to print out threatening messages and hacking office cameras for use in a propaganda video released in early October. That video included a taunt in French referencing ongoing education-related protests, and came just before the attacks on French supermarket fridges. Cyber incident response firm Profero attributed the Israel attack to a wing of Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps .

Over the summer, commissaries on U.S. military bases also went through something similar, when food spoiled after the temperature shot up inside refrigerators and freezers overnight.

The French government is the first to formally assign blame for the wave of destructive attacks.

They were able to identify the hackers through a series of digital clues, including digital infrastructure used by the hackers, connection to a propaganda outlet, and "traces" of the use of Farsi language in the attack, according to ANSSI .

While NPR and others have reported that U.S. officials suspect Iran may have been behind the attacks on U.S. military bases in August, the Pentagon has not made any official statement, even to conclude that the disruptions were in fact the result of a cyberattack.

"Consistent with our policy and to preserve the integrity of the process, the DOD [Office of Inspector General] Criminal Investigative Service does not discuss ongoing investigations," Mollie Halpern, a spokesperson for the Department of War Office of the Inspector General wrote in an email to NPR.

If Iranian hackers are behind the attacks across Europe, the U.S. and Israel, cybersecurity experts say that would fit with what they know about Iranian hackers' strategy and goals.

"Iran's cyberattacks against refrigeration systems likely represents the IRGC attempting to reassert Iranian power abroad through both physically and psychologically disruptive operations," Alex Orleans, the head of threat intelligence at cybersecurity firm Sublime Security, told NPR. "Such activities continue to provide tangible and cost-effect results given how Iran's national resources remain tied down in the war."

"Also, Shahid Kaveh, the IRGC cyber unit that the French specifically attributed the disruptive attacks to, is repeating a pattern here," Orleans says. He referenced a series of cyberattacks on American water treatment plants in August, which most experts believe were linked to Iran, as precedent. The U.S. government has still not officially attributed those attacks.

"This unit has once again refined its tradecraft through attacks on Israeli targets before shifting their targeting to the same systems in the West," Orleans says.

For those tracking Shahid Kaveh and the other Iranian cyber units that operate alongside it, these attacks fit squarely into their modus operandi.

"Shahid Kaveh group is an offensive cyber unit responsible for some of the greatest hits of Iranian offensive cyber [operations]," says Ari Ben Am, an adjunct fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies' Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation.

One group tied to Shahid Kaveh is the Cyber Av3ngers, he explains, which the U.S. government linked to cyberattacks on Israeli-made systems in U.S. water treatment facilities in the winter between 2023 and 2024. The French government also cited other cyberattacks carried out on behalf of the IRGC against French interests, including against the satirical French magazine Charlie Hebdo and another against digital kiosks used at the Paris Olympics in 2024.

Cybersecurity experts say the attacks on refrigeration controllers have highlighted a yearslong difficulty with securing operational technology, the machines that control physical processes in the real world — from water pumps to cooling systems.

These machines are often outdated and riddled with vulnerabilities, and are very difficult to patch because operators can't afford to shut them down and disrupt critical services including healthcare and transportation. Additionally, the machines are often left exposed to the open internet — often at least in part due to contractual requirements with vendors that want to maintain those systems remotely. That combination of factors makes it a complicated problem to solve .

Iran has yet to respond to the accusations. However, Monday's accusation by the French government may lead other affected countries to take action as well.

During Monday's G7 meeting in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked by journalists whether the U.S. shared information with the French to help with their attribution of the Iranian hacks. Rubio said he couldn't comment, but noted that the "French are quite capable."

"What kind of sickos are these people?" he asked. "They attack refrigerators. France is not even involved in this, really," referring to the war between the U.S. and Iran, which began in February. "[These Iranians] do terrible things around the world … the news today doesn't surprise us," Rubio concluded.

item.title: Apocalyptic sci-fi novel 'The End of Everything' wins this year's Booker Prize

item.content:encoded:
The End of Everything by British author M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize. In a statement, Mary Beard, chair of this year's judges, called it a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism."

The satirical sci-fi novel follows Philip, a man who looks for "artifacts" along the coast in Kent, England, and his aunt Marnie. The book is set in a post-apocalyptic future, dealing with the slow-burning invasion of the shape-shifting iGhetti.

In an interview with the Booker Prize team, Harrison said he drew inspiration from current affairs: "What happens when all of our expectations and explanations of the world become an ongoing disaster, but we still have to make a life?"

At 81, Harrison is the oldest author to win in the history of the prize. He's had a decades-long writing career, with Everything being his 13th novel. Most of his career has been spent writing science fiction. His 2006 novel, Nova Swing , won both the Arthur C. Clarke and Philip K. Dick awards (which reward the best in science fiction in the U.K. and U.S., respectively).

"Many past Booker Prize authors have borrowed facets of science fiction in their work," wrote Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, in a statement. "But M. John Harrison is the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world. He is a genuinely original thinker, a genre-defying writer who takes ideas seriously."

The Booker Prize honors the best fiction published in the U.K. and Ireland. Besides Beard, this year's judges included the poet Raymond Antrobus, Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, editor and critic Rebecca Liu, and poet and novelist Patricia Lockwood. The other books shortlisted for the prize this year included Marlon James' The Disappearers and The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout.

Winners of the prize receive £50,000 (about $67,000), and a trophy presented by the previous year's winner. Author David Szalay won the 2025 prize with his novel Flesh.

item.title: Supreme Court says border wall construction can continue in west Texas

item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to continue with its plans to construct hundreds of miles of border barrier and security infrastructure in west Texas, while a court hearing over the effort moves forward.

The federal government's plans have stirred bipartisan backlash for its inclusion of Big Bend National Park, a beloved stretch of public land known for its sweeping canyons and unspoiled desert landscape.

In a five-page decision issued Monday , the high court wrote that the federal judge who ruled on the order didn't have the authority to weigh in.

"The injunction thus impedes the Government from advancing its 'compelling interests' in border security and integrity," reads the unsigned decision. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter in the decision.

The court wrote that federal law allows the Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to waive environmental protections and conservation laws, which they called a "clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert."

In an emergency application to the high court in late October , the federal government urged the justices to intervene and allow the work to begin again, saying that a gap in "border defenses" in the Big Bend region "would act as "a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors."

A federal judge in El Paso issued the temporary injunction that halted the construction of 30-foot-tall steel barriers, patrol roads, surveillance systems and other border infrastructure.

The Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental advocacy group, brought forward the lawsuit, along with an area nonprofit working to preserve a historic church near the U.S.-Mexico border and a landowner who stands to lose his border property.

"This decision greenlights the contractors and allows the bulldozers to come roaring back into the region," said Laiken Jordahl with the Center for Biological Diversity. "It allows the dynamiting of national park canyon walls, the bulldozing of pristine desert."

The lawsuit argued that the Department of Homeland Security's plans are unconstitutional and that Big Bend residents would be "irreparably harmed" if the construction continues.

The Trump administration's plans for the beloved Big Bend region of Texas have provoked an unusual bipartisan backlash. People across the political spectrum say a wall isn't needed in the Big Bend––a region known for its sweeping canyons, tough terrain and unforgiving desert heat. They worry about the threats a wall or any other kind of infrastructure poses to the region, from the impact on the environment and Indigenous sites to the effect on the region's tourism-based economy and on wild animals .

In the Trump administration's emergency relief request to the Supreme Court , Solicitor General John Sauer called the injunction "baseless" and "unprecedented" and said any pocket of the Big Bend without a barrier would "become a funnel point for illegal alien crossings that are thwarted by barriers elsewhere."

Historically, the Big Bend area's rugged landscape has meant fewer people attempting to cross into the U.S. through this pocket of the border. And while the Big Bend Sector, a nearly 500-mile stretch covered by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, makes up over a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border, it regularly sees the fewest number of encounters along the Texas border, according to CBP data .

item.title: Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
item.description: Updated November 10, 2026 at 10:17 AM ChST Rep. Thomas Massie has reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting up a vote in the House of Representatives in the next two days.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 10, 2026 at 10:17 AM ChST

Rep. Thomas Massie has reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting up a vote in the House of Representatives in the next two days.

The Kentucky Republican's resolution accuses Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors and lists eight specific charges against him.

Hegseth defended his record at the Pentagon in a video released last Thursday, dismissing Massie's effort as "sham articles of impeachment."

"Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me," Hegseth said.

Speaking to reporters during an impromptu press briefing on Monday, Trump expressed support for his embattled Defense Secretary.

"I'll stand by him," Trump said. "He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won."

Massie has long been a staunch critic of Hegseth. During the GOP primary, Hegseth campaigned on behalf of Ed Gallrein, who went on to defeat Massie.

In response to Hegseth calling him a "disgruntled defeated congressman," Massie told reporters on Monday: "Well, he's right about one thing — I'm a defeated congressman. I'm not disgruntled."

He added: "I'm being polite here. What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing someone, really. You don't go to prison, you don't go to jail, you don't pay a fine. When the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious."

Massie said the effort also underscores the need to litigate whether Congress has real war powers or not. The war powers resolution has largely been ignored by presidents of both parties.

"What's at heart here is the balance of power between the executive branch and Congress," he said.

Massie first sought to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterm elections , prompting Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to call an early recess to avoid the vote. That caused the resolution to expire, which is why Massie reintroduced the resolution Monday.

Presumptive next House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has already signaled support for an impeachment push against Hegseth.

Even Republican members who oppose impeaching Hegseth have said the Trump administration could do a better job making the case to Congress and the public about what the plan is for the Iran war going forward.

Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio., indicated to NPR that impeachment would be hypocritical given that administrations going back to the Korean War have largely ignored Congress' war powers efforts.

"I think trying to scapegoat Pete Hegseth is just the status quo politics in Washington," he said. "I think it would be a mistake to impeach."

Davidson said lawmakers who want changes are better off trying to leverage the power of the purse to withhold money from the conflict.

There could be sufficient votes to impeach Hegseth in the House, with the support of all Democrats, Massie, and a handful of Republicans. However, it is unlikely to clear the higher Senate threshold for convicting and removing Hegseth from office — which requires two-thirds of the Senate.

NPR's Eric McDaniel contributed to this report.
